title: VPSHR Level 0
description: A responsive learning pathway for the Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights, built around the published VPSHR course files already stored in this repository.
audience: Security teams, site leaders, contractors, and employees who need a practical baseline in human rights responsibilities.
integrationNotes: Each Next.js learning unit can be embedded or linked from Thinkific.
The original iSpring exports remain available under public/courses/vpshr-level-0 for compatibility.
Progress is saved locally as a placeholder until a Thinkific or LMS API is connected.

units.title: Introduction to VPSHR Level 0
units.subtitle: Set the context for rights-aware security practice.
objectives: Recognize why security and human rights belong in the same operating conversation.
Identify how the course is structured and how each learning unit builds on the last.
Connect the VPSHR baseline to everyday workplace decision-making.

slides.title: Course purpose
slides.body: This pathway introduces VPSHR as a practical operating standard for respectful, accountable security.

slides.title: Learner commitment
slides.body: Learners are asked to connect each topic to real choices they may make on site or in the field.

quiz.prompt: VPSHR training only applies to specialist legal teams.
quiz.feedback: VPSHR awareness is relevant to security personnel, employees, contractors, managers, and leaders.

survey.prompt: Where could human rights risks appear in your day-to-day security environment?
survey.guidance: Name one practical setting, such as access control, protest response, contractor supervision, or incident reporting.

summary: Security decisions can affect dignity, safety, and trust.
The rest of the course turns the VPSHR baseline into practical scenarios and checks.

units.title: Definition of Human Rights
units.subtitle: Build a shared vocabulary for rights and responsibilities.
objectives: Define human rights in plain operational language.
Recognize that rights apply to everyone without discrimination.
Explain why rights awareness matters in private and public security settings.

slides.title: Universal rights
slides.body: Human rights protect the dignity and safety of every person affected by security operations.

slides.title: Operational relevance
slides.body: The definition becomes practical when teams use it to guide communication, escalation, and reporting.

slides.title: Accountability
slides.body: Respect for rights depends on preparation, supervision, and consistent follow-through.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best describes human rights in this training context?

options.label: Standards that protect dignity, safety, and fair treatment
Benefits that only apply after a legal complaint
Internal company preferences with no operational effect

quiz.feedback: The course treats human rights as practical standards that guide how people are treated during security operations.

survey.prompt: A visitor is frustrated at a checkpoint and raises their voice. What is the best first response?

options.label: Listen, de-escalate, and explain the process
Ignore the concern and move to enforcement

survey.guidance: A rights-aware response starts with calm communication and proportionate action.

summary: Human rights are not abstract extras; they shape everyday security choices.
Clear definitions help teams make consistent decisions under pressure.

units.title: Responsibilities
units.subtitle: Clarify who carries which responsibilities in a VPSHR environment.
objectives: Identify employee, contractor, security, and leadership responsibilities.
Distinguish personal conduct from organizational accountability.
Recognize when concerns should be escalated or reported.

slides.title: Shared responsibility
slides.body: Rights-aware security works when every role understands its part.

slides.title: Escalation points
slides.body: Early escalation prevents small concerns from becoming serious incidents.

slides.title: Record and learn
slides.body: Accurate reporting supports accountability and continuous improvement.

quiz.prompt: Which actions support responsible VPSHR implementation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Report credible concerns through the correct channel
Keep security teams trained and supervised
Avoid documenting incidents to reduce paperwork

quiz.feedback: Responsible implementation depends on training, reporting, supervision, and review.

survey.prompt: What responsibility in your role most directly affects another person's dignity or safety?
survey.guidance: Focus on one task where communication, supervision, or escalation matters.

summary: Responsibilities must be visible before an incident happens.
Documentation, escalation, and supervision are core safeguards.

units.title: Benefits of Human Rights
units.subtitle: Connect rights practice to trust, resilience, and safer operations.
objectives: Describe how rights-aware conduct improves community trust.
Recognize operational benefits of de-escalation and fair treatment.
Link better security outcomes to accountability.

slides.title: Trust lowers risk
slides.body: Respectful engagement can reduce tension and improve the quality of information shared with security teams.

slides.title: Consistency matters
slides.body: People are more likely to cooperate when rules are explained and applied fairly.

slides.title: Better decisions
slides.body: Rights-aware teams are more likely to choose proportionate, defensible actions.

quiz.prompt: Match each practice to its likely benefit.
quiz.feedback: Human rights practice has operational value when it is applied consistently.

survey.prompt: A community member reports rough treatment by a contractor. Which benefit is most at risk if the concern is ignored?
survey.guidance: Trust is damaged when people believe concerns will not be heard or addressed.

summary: Human rights practice helps prevent harm and strengthens trust.
Operational benefits depend on consistent behavior, not slogans.

units.title: Thirty Human Rights
units.subtitle: Explore the rights baseline behind VPSHR decision-making.
objectives: Recognize that rights cover safety, liberty, equality, privacy, and fair treatment.
Connect broad rights language to security touchpoints.
Identify when a right may be affected by an operational decision.

slides.title: Rights families
slides.body: Human rights include civil, political, economic, social, and cultural protections.

slides.title: Security touchpoints
slides.body: Access control, searches, investigations, and protest response can all affect rights.

slides.title: Proportionate action
slides.body: Security measures should be necessary, lawful, and proportionate to the risk.

quiz.feedback: Proportionate security action should be lawful and necessary before force or restrictions are considered.

survey.prompt: Choose one right that could be affected during a site security incident.
survey.guidance: Consider privacy, personal safety, freedom of movement, or fair treatment.

summary: Human rights give security teams a practical standard for evaluating impact.
Necessity and proportionality are central decision checks.

units.subtitle: Spot early indicators before incidents escalate.

slides.title: Context signals
slides.body: Conflict, community tension, weak supervision, and unclear rules can increase the likelihood of harm.
slides.thumbnail: /courses/vpshr-level-0/LU5 Factors-contributing/5. Basic human rights-final (Published)/6. Factors that may contribute-final (Published)/data/thmb1.jpg

slides.title: Behavior signals
slides.body: Aggressive language, intimidation, and unmanaged bias can turn routine security tasks into rights risks.
slides.thumbnail: /courses/vpshr-level-0/LU5 Factors-contributing/5. Basic human rights-final (Published)/6. Factors that may contribute-final (Published)/data/thmb2.jpg

slides.title: Control signals
slides.body: Training, supervision, and clear escalation paths are practical controls.
slides.thumbnail: /courses/vpshr-level-0/LU5 Factors-contributing/5. Basic human rights-final (Published)/6. Factors that may contribute-final (Published)/data/thmb3.jpg

quiz.prompt: Which situation is an early warning sign for human rights risk?

options.label: Unclear instructions during a tense community interaction
A calm briefing with documented escalation channels

quiz.feedback: Unclear instructions during tension can lead to inconsistent, disproportionate, or harmful responses.

survey.prompt: Name one factor that could raise rights risk at your site.
survey.guidance: Think about context, behavior, training, supervision, or reporting channels.

summary: Risk factors are easier to manage when they are identified early.
Controls should be practical, documented, and understood before incidents occur.

units.title: Role of Employees
units.subtitle: Make human rights awareness part of everyday conduct.
objectives: Recognize the employee role in identifying and escalating concerns.
Apply respectful conduct during interactions with colleagues, contractors, and communities.
Use available reporting channels when something does not look right.

slides.title: Speak up early
slides.body: Employees can prevent harm by raising concerns before they escalate.

slides.title: Respectful conduct
slides.body: Every interaction is an opportunity to reinforce dignity and fairness.

slides.title: Know the channel
slides.body: Reports are more useful when employees know where to send them and what details matter.

quiz.prompt: Only supervisors can raise human rights concerns.
quiz.feedback: Every employee has a role in recognizing and escalating credible concerns.

survey.prompt: You see a colleague mocking a community member during a tense interaction. What should you do?

options.label: Use a safe intervention or report through the proper channel
Ignore it because it is not your job
Join in to keep the team aligned

survey.guidance: Employees should act safely and use the correct escalation route when conduct may affect dignity or safety.

summary: Employees are often closest to early warning signs.
Respectful conduct and reporting channels are practical safeguards.

units.title: Key Policy Requirements
units.subtitle: Turn policy commitments into working controls.
objectives: Identify the policy elements that support VPSHR implementation.
Link policy requirements to training, incident management, and contractor oversight.
Recognize how documentation supports accountability.

slides.title: Policy to practice
slides.body: Requirements only protect people when teams can apply them in daily work.

slides.title: Contractor oversight
slides.body: External security providers need the same clarity, training, and supervision.

slides.title: Incident learning
slides.body: Policies should help teams record, investigate, and improve after incidents.

quiz.prompt: Which items belong in a practical VPSHR policy framework?
quiz.feedback: Policy requirements should make training, reporting, supervision, and oversight clear.

survey.prompt: Which policy requirement would most help your team act consistently?
survey.guidance: Choose a control that would reduce uncertainty during a real interaction.

summary: Policy requirements need practical owners and routines.
Training, reporting, and contractor oversight make the requirements usable.

units.title: Voluntary Principles on Security and Human Rights
units.subtitle: Understand the VPSHR framework and its operating expectations.
objectives: Describe the purpose of VPSHR.
Identify how risk assessment, public security, and private security fit together.
Connect VPSHR expectations to site-level controls.

slides.title: Framework pillars
slides.body: VPSHR connects risk assessment, public security, and private security management.

slides.title: Risk assessment
slides.body: The framework starts with understanding context and likely impacts.

slides.title: Security partners
slides.body: The framework expects appropriate engagement, training, and accountability across security providers.

quiz.prompt: Match each VPSHR area to the practical question it raises.

pairs.right: What context and impacts should we anticipate?
How do we engage state security actors responsibly?
How do we train and oversee contracted providers?

quiz.feedback: VPSHR becomes operational when each area is tied to practical questions and controls.

survey.prompt: Which VPSHR area feels most relevant to your current site context?
survey.guidance: Choose risk assessment, public security, or private security and explain why.

summary: VPSHR is a management framework for rights-aware security.
The framework expects practical controls across risk, public security, and private security.

units.title: Role of Security
units.subtitle: Apply VPSHR expectations to security team conduct.
objectives: Explain the role of security in protecting people and assets responsibly.
Apply de-escalation, proportionality, and reporting expectations.
Recognize when additional support or supervision is needed.

slides.title: Protective posture
slides.body: Security teams protect people, property, and rights when they act with discipline and respect.

slides.title: De-escalation
slides.body: Calm communication and measured action can prevent avoidable harm.

slides.title: Accountability
slides.body: Security actions should be explainable, documented, and open to review.

quiz.prompt: A security response should be proportionate to the actual risk.
quiz.feedback: Proportionality is one of the key checks for rights-aware security action.

survey.prompt: A small group gathers near an access gate to complain about employment concerns. What should security prioritize first?

options.label: Immediate force to disperse the group

survey.guidance: A proportionate first response focuses on safety, communication, and escalation.

summary: Security teams are guardians of both safety and respectful treatment.
De-escalation, proportionality, and documentation support accountable security.

units.title: Investigations
units.subtitle: Handle security investigations with fairness and care.
objectives: Identify rights risks in security investigations.
Apply fairness, privacy, and non-retaliation principles.
Recognize when investigation concerns should be escalated.

slides.title: Fair process
slides.body: Investigations should gather facts without intimidation, discrimination, or retaliation.

slides.title: Privacy
slides.body: Information should be handled only by people with a legitimate role in the process.

slides.title: Follow-through
slides.body: Findings should lead to appropriate action and learning.

quiz.prompt: Which practice best supports a rights-aware investigation?

options.label: Collect facts fairly and protect sensitive information

quiz.feedback: Fairness, privacy, and careful documentation reduce investigation risk.

survey.prompt: What information should be protected during an investigation?
survey.guidance: Consider identity, allegations, evidence, medical details, and witness information.

summary: Investigations can create rights risks if handled carelessly.
Fairness, privacy, and non-retaliation should shape each step.

units.title: Civil Unrest
units.subtitle: Prepare for protest and unrest scenarios with restraint.
objectives: Recognize rights risks during protest, unrest, or crowd scenarios.
Apply de-escalation and proportionality principles.
Understand when to coordinate with appropriate public authorities.

slides.title: Safety first
slides.body: Civil unrest planning should protect people while respecting lawful expression and movement.

slides.title: Clear roles
slides.body: Private security roles should be defined before public security actors become involved.

slides.title: Restraint
slides.body: Force, restrictions, and dispersal should never be default responses.

quiz.prompt: Which actions support a rights-aware response to unrest?

options.label: Use force as the default first action

quiz.feedback: Preparation, communication, documentation, and restraint support rights-aware response.

survey.prompt: A protest becomes louder but remains non-violent. What should security review before escalating?

options.label: Actual risk, roles, communication, and proportionality

survey.guidance: Escalation decisions should be based on actual risk and proportionate response.

summary: Civil unrest response requires planning, restraint, and clear roles.
Rights-aware teams distinguish disruption from genuine safety risk.

units.title: Surveillance and Monitoring
units.subtitle: Balance security monitoring with privacy and accountability.
objectives: Identify privacy risks linked to surveillance and monitoring.
Apply necessity, purpose limitation, and access control principles.
Recognize when monitoring activity should be reviewed or escalated.

slides.title: Purpose limitation
slides.body: Monitoring should be tied to a legitimate security purpose.

slides.title: Privacy controls
slides.body: Access to monitoring data should be limited, logged, and reviewed.

slides.title: Transparency
slides.body: People should know when monitoring affects them unless a legitimate exception applies.

quiz.prompt: What is the best first check before using surveillance data?

options.label: Confirm a legitimate purpose and authorized access
Use it if someone is curious
Share it widely to save time

quiz.feedback: Monitoring data should be used only for legitimate purposes by authorized people.

survey.prompt: What privacy control would be most important for monitoring at your site?
survey.guidance: Consider access limits, retention, signage, review, or incident logs.

summary: Surveillance can support safety but can also affect privacy and trust.
Legitimate purpose, limited access, and review are core controls.
